assumptions.summary: Intercepted messages and topics truthfully represent thoughts.
Suspicious topics and contact with known conspirators raise likelihood.
Known conspirators occupy important positions and can serve as criteria.
All workers can be represented on a zero-to-one suspiciousness scale.
Node-level communication can be treated as bidirectional even when messages are directed.
Outgoing suspicious communication is more informative than passive receipt.
Partner labels can be coded as 1, 0.5, or 0.
Topic, partner, and direction priorities can be represented by 6,3,1 AHP judgments.
Only the joint-high centrality/CIC quadrant contains conspirators.
Four topic-description features adequately proxy unavailable message text.
The four semantic features have equal importance.
The inferred 28-person subnetwork is suitable for leader and activity analysis.

data_and_preprocessing.summary: The paper states 82 workers but elsewhere prioritizes 83, with seven known conspirators and eight known non-conspirators.
Delores and Dolores are merged as one person.
One of five duplicate-name Elsie records is chosen as the known conspirator.
Workers become nodes; messages become directed edges; topic class becomes edge weight.
Topic, partner identity, and sender/receiver direction become CIC fields.
Known labels and Topics 7,11,13 populate Requirement 1.
A new person/topic clue is substituted into the same model.
Four binary features are extracted from topic descriptions because raw messages are unavailable.
The analysis forms a subnetwork from the reported 28 inferred conspirators.

abstract previews one response per requirement: Open with the operational difficulty, then give the method, displayed result, comparison, refinement, downstream analysis, and final scope in requirement order.

introduction converts a broad investigation into two decisions: Move from domain difficulty to the available message database, state the bounded population, then separate member identification from leader detection.
a limitation checklist motivates a local model expansion: Describe the prior model family, enumerate missing content, direction, mixed identities, and link effects, then name the required expansion.
data defects are made visible before working rules: Name a spelling collision, duplicate identity, or anomalous self-message, state the local rule used, and keep the decision upstream of modeling.

problem analysis separates node and link viewpoints before synthesis: Define what the node view captures, define what message edges add, explain the mapping from domain concepts to graph objects, then combine both views.

existing network assumptions are contrasted with the local case: List where standard criminal networks differ, retain reusable structure, introduce mixed identity probabilities, and state the local direction treatment.
plain-language network intuition precedes normalized formulas: Explain what degree, betweenness, or closeness means operationally, account for network size, then present the normalized expression.
message semantics become a three-factor edge score: Name topic, conversation partner, and direction, assign each a bounded coding rule, combine them for one edge, then aggregate over a person.
qualitative importance statements are converted to AHP weights: Order the factors in prose, expose the comparison scores and matrix, solve the weight vector, and report the consistency result.
node centrality and criminal information are fused into one score: Restate what each component represents, justify the chosen interaction, display the system, rescale it, and name the cutoff rule.
four qualitative score quadrants explain the decision logic: Cross low/high centrality with low/high information, interpret each quadrant, and reserve the positive class for the joint-high case.
a simple case is used before the full network: State known labels and topics, run the model, compare named outputs with the reference analysis, count disagreements, and interpret the leader result.
a displayed ranking is translated into a bounded next decision: Read the leading score or rank, compare known labels, state the candidate count, then identify the review or leader action.

a second method is presented under shared features before comparison: State the baseline formula, list the shared features, display both outputs, and compare classification, ranking, network use, and small-sample behavior.

new evidence is inserted through parameter substitution and rerun: State the changed clue, retain the model structure, substitute the affected parameters, display old and new ranks, and explain directional changes.

an admitted binary-topic loss triggers semantic refinement: Name the information lost by a two-class topic label, introduce text or semantic analysis, define the intended feature representation, and connect it to the edge weight.

missing raw text causes a transparent proxy-feature substitution: Declare that original messages are unavailable, use topic descriptions instead, define interpretable binary fields, choose coefficients, and keep the approximation visible.

text-derived weights are compared against the previous run: Display the topic-weight table, explain changed groups, rerun the same model, report paired ranks or scores, and state what did and did not change.

network metrics are handed to concrete investigative actions: Define a network property, read an exact plotted or tabulated value, interpret the limited structural implication, then name a targeted follow-up action.

paper-specific results are abstracted into a reusable workflow: Separate common network properties from domain-specific edge information, transform both into indexes, combine them into a score, and close with limitations and future work.

title: Extended Criminal Network Analysis Model Allows Conspirators Nowhere to Hide
unresolved_questions: The official task statement is unavailable, so requirements are reconstructed only from the paper's Abstract, Introduction, and section headings.
Abstract claims about accuracy, stability, superiority, larger suspect sets, and average score growth are paper-internal previews without independent reproduction.
The paper alternates between 82 and 83 workers, leaving the candidate-population denominator unresolved.
Duplicate names are resolved locally without external identifiers, and choosing one Elsie as known may alter labels and network structure.
The self-message for Node 3 is deleted as strange without an error log, provenance check, or sensitivity alternative.
The truthfulness assumption conflicts with the paper's own example that people may lie during intercepted communication.
Direction is ignored in node-level adjacency even though direction is later treated as identity-relevant in CIC.
Unknown people are called suspicious conspirators with values between zero and one, but those values are not calibrated probabilities.
Centrality orientation, shortest-path counting, normalization, disconnected paths, and the division by the source closeness-like distance are not justified.
The betweenness indicator records whether a shortest path passes through a node but does not handle multiple equal shortest paths.
The symbol table defines v inconsistently as a node count while formulas use v as a node identity.
CIC switches among W1, W(v), f/g/h, and topic-weight notation without a complete symbol-domain contract.
Outgoing direction is coded 1 and incoming 0.5, while partner identity is coded 1, 0.5, or 0 without empirical estimation.
AHP inputs 6, 3, and 1 are subjective; perfect matrix consistency follows their construction and does not validate predictive relevance.
Multiplying centrality by CIC, rescaling by the maximum, and choosing the largest slope change as cutoff lack calibration and stability analysis.
The EZ discussion says one person is misjudged but reports an 80% error rate, contradicting the Abstract's 20% and the implied one-of-five arithmetic.
Agreement with a supervisor who also missed and misjudged people is not independent validation.
The full-network claim of about 80% accuracy and 23 conspirators lacks ground truth for the unknown workers and a declared denominator.
Gretchen is promoted to an identified conspirator because of managerial status and high model rank, creating circular label use.
The Fisher comparison does not freeze matched preprocessing, tuning, thresholds, duplicated identities, or a common error metric.
The stated failure of Fisher on the small EZ case is not accompanied by conditioning diagnostics, regularization, or an alternative baseline.
The new-clue section says the suspect count reduces to 28 from 23, an arithmetic direction contradiction also reflected in the Abstract's 21.7% increase.
Original messages are unavailable, so topic descriptions proxy for message-level semantic and text analysis.
Equal 0.25 feature coefficients are imposed for convenience without sensitivity, annotation reliability, or learned weights.
The prose says one table replaces 0.9 and 0.1 but table numbering and the prior binary-weight contract are inconsistent.
Text-analysis results report 18 versus 16 flagged people, while other sections use 23 or 28, without a stable cohort or scenario key.
Both text and non-text runs retain a 20% misjudgment rate, so higher scores and more flagged people do not demonstrate better accuracy.
The depth-analysis subnetwork uses 28 inferred conspirators immediately after the text-analysis section reports 18, with no reconciliation.
The unnormalized leader-score sum is dominated by degree, has no threshold or leader labels, and nominates Sherri despite earlier sections naming Elsie.
Figure 9 contains corrupted '/generic format' axis labels, preventing faithful reading of the vertical scale.
The generalized workflow proposes a weighted average even though the paper's ECNAM combines centrality and CIC by a product.
Claims of perfect experiential match, credibility, rationality, correctness, and extendability are unsupported by independent tests.
Criminal psychology, deception, and unclear classification criteria are acknowledged only after decisions have already been reported.
Future work repeats semantic analysis as prospective even though the preceding section presents it as already applied, leaving implementation status ambiguous.

writing_logic.summary: difficulty -> requirement -> method -> exact result -> comparison -> refinement -> scope
domain stakes -> message data -> bounded population -> member and leader questions
prior SNA -> four missing elements -> need for extension
visible name/self-loop defects -> explicit local rules -> downstream model
node viewpoint + practical edge viewpoint -> graph mapping -> hybrid
standard-network mismatch -> retained SNA structure -> local mixed-label adaptation
metric meaning -> network-size concern -> normalized formula
topic/partner/direction intuitions -> coding -> edge CIC -> person CIC
importance order -> AHP scores -> matrix -> weights -> consistency
centrality meaning + CIC meaning -> product -> rescaling -> cutoff
two axes -> four quadrants -> joint-high class
simple inputs -> figure -> named disagreements -> leader reading
Fisher formula -> shared features -> paired tables -> capability comparison
new clue -> parameter substitution -> old/new visual -> directional explanation
binary topic loss -> semantic method -> feature fields -> c1 handoff
raw text absent -> topic-description proxy -> equal coefficients -> visible boundary
weight table -> topic groups -> same-model rerun -> paired scores
metric definition -> exact value -> structural interpretation -> investigation action
common properties + domain-specific features -> indexes -> combined score -> general workflow
claimed strengths -> admitted psychology/cutoff limits -> future repairs
